---
title: "A chain you can rewire"
---

Your playlist holds 300 songs and the newest one belongs at the top. An array
puts it there with one call, `unshift`, and behind that call it moves all 300
songs one slot to the right to make room. This part builds the same playlist out
of small boxes that point at each other, where a song joins the top by rewiring
exactly one arrow.

Hand-built data structures are new for the coding buddy as well. Part 7 has one
that knows about nodes, head pointers, and the tail pointer a queue needs, and
its key replaces the Part 6 key in `~/.pi/agent/auth.json`
(@sec-buddy-setup-new-part).

{{< coding coding-buddy-data-structures >}}

## The price of the front {#sec-linked-list-experiment}

{{< exercise playlist tests=true >}}

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `coursework/`, in a folder
   called `playlist`. This app carries the whole chapter, and the next chapter
   opens it again.

2. Delete `src/math.ts` and `src/math.test.ts`, and replace everything in
   `src/index.ts` with one line:

   ```ts
   import './styles.css';
   ```

3. Under that line, fill two arrays with the same 100,000 numbers. The first one
   grows at the end, the second one grows at the front:

   ```ts
   const COUNT = 100_000;

   const atEnd: number[] = [];
   const endStart = performance.now();
   for (let i = 0; i < COUNT; i++) {
     atEnd.push(i);
   }
   console.log(`push:    ${(performance.now() - endStart).toFixed(1)} ms`);

   const atFront: number[] = [];
   const frontStart = performance.now();
   for (let i = 0; i < COUNT; i++) {
     atFront.unshift(i);
   }
   console.log(`unshift: ${(performance.now() - frontStart).toFixed(1)} ms`);
   ```

   `performance.now()` hands you a number of milliseconds, so the difference
   between two of them is how long the loop took. The underscores in `100_000`
   are for your eyes only, and TypeScript reads that as 100000.

4. Run `npm start` and open the browser console with F12. The page shows an
   empty playlist for now, and the console carries the answer:

   ```text
   push:    5.3 ms
   unshift: 263.4 ms
   ```

Your two numbers will look different, and that is fine. The ratio is the point.
Both loops inserted the same 100,000 numbers, and the loop that inserted at the
front took about fifty times as long.

## What the array is paying for {#sec-linked-list-costs}

An array keeps its items in one block, in order, so the item at index 7 is
always exactly seven slots from the start. That is why reading by index is
instant. It is also why `unshift` is slow: there is no free slot in front of
index 0, so every item in the array shifts one slot to the right to open one.
With 100,000 items in the array, one `unshift` moves 100,000 items.

A **linked list** gives that block up. It uses one small box per item, and each
box holds the item plus the location of the next box. The boxes may sit anywhere
in memory. A new item joins the front by building one box that points at the old
first box, and nothing else moves at all.

|                              | Array                                | Linked list                                   |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| Read the item at position 7  | one step, whatever the length        | start at the front and take seven steps       |
| Insert or remove at the front | move every item one slot            | build or unhook one box                       |
| Insert or remove in the middle | find the spot fast, then move the rest | walk to the spot, then change two arrows  |
| Memory                       | one block, in one piece              | one box per item, and a pointer inside each box |

Read that table as a trade and not as a scoreboard. An array is the right answer
for a high score table you read by rank and rewrite once a game. A linked list
is the right answer when items keep arriving and leaving at the ends and nobody
ever asks for item number 40. Almost every collection you built this year was
right to be an array, and Part 7 closes by making that choice on purpose instead
of by habit.

People who compare structures for a living write these costs in a short
notation, `O(1)` for "one step whatever the size" and `O(n)` for "a step per
item". You will meet it in every algorithms book, and a search for "Big O
notation" explains it in five minutes.

## Boxes with a pointer in them {#sec-linked-list-node}

The box is called a **node**, and this is the whole class:

```ts
class Node<T> {
  value: T;
  next: Node<T> | null = null;

  constructor(value: T) {
    this.value = value;
  }
}
```

A node carries exactly two things. `value` is the item, and `next` is the node
that comes after this one. The type parameter `T` is there for the same reason
`Stack<T>` has one in @sec-generics-type-parameter: a node has no opinion about
what it carries, and the moment it says `Song` it can never carry anything
else. Every structure in this part writes its own `Node<T>` again.

The `| null` is the interesting half. The last node in the chain has nothing
after it, and something has to go into `next` anyway. Take the `| null` away and
TypeScript refuses the class before you have written a single method:

```text
src/playlist.ts(3,3): error TS2564: Property 'next' has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor.
```

So `null` moves in as the end marker, and it answers the only question a walk
ever asks: is there another node, or am I done?

The list class itself remembers one single node, the first one, in a field
called the **head**. An empty list has `head === null`.

![A playlist of three songs: the head points at the first node, every node
points at the next one, and the last node has `null` in its `next`
field.](list-chain.svg){width=720}

Every arrow in that picture is a **pointer**, the word programmers everywhere
use for "this box knows where that box is". Nowhere in the picture is there an
index or a length. To reach the third song you start at `head` and follow `next`
twice, and that walk is the move every method below is built from.

`Node` is not exported: it lives in the same file as the structure that uses it,
the way the three command classes shared `src/command.ts` in @sec-undo-command.
Nobody outside the playlist ever holds a node, so nobody outside needs the class.

::: {.research title="Three things the playlist needs from you"}
The tests you write next check for a missing song, the wiring at the end of the
chapter fills a dropdown from your playlist, and the arrows in the diagram above
carry a name with a history. MDN and the Vitest documentation have all three
answers, and nothing after this box gives any of them away.

1. Two of your playlist tests check that `find` gave nothing back. Which Vitest
   matcher checks that a value is exactly `null`? And what is the difference
   between `null` and `undefined` in JavaScript?
2. The **Insert after** dropdown is empty in `index.html`, and your code fills
   it. Which element does `document.createElement('option')` hand you, and which
   two properties do you set on it so that the dropdown shows a song title and
   gives that same title back through `select.value`?
3. The word **pointer** comes from languages such as C. What is a pointer there?
   And when TypeScript runs `newNode.next = this.head;`, does the node on the
   right get copied into `next`, or do both names then mean the very same node?

Question 3 is exam material. Every rewiring in this part stands or falls on that
one sentence, and the exam has no internet and no AI.
:::

## The playlist on an array {#sec-linked-list-array}

The interface comes first, and an array is the fastest way to pin it down. You
write the tests, make them pass with `Song[]` inside the class, and then swap the
insides for nodes without touching a single test. If the tests survive that, the
interface was the real thing and the array was just an early guess about how to
store the songs.

1. Create `src/playlist.test.ts` with the first sentence about a class that does
   not exist yet:

   ```ts
   import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
   import { Playlist } from './playlist';

   describe('Playlist', () => {
     it('starts with no songs', () => {
       const playlist = new Playlist();

       expect(playlist.toArray()).toEqual([]);
     });
   });
   ```

2. Run `npm test`:

   ```text
    ❯ src/playlist.test.ts (0 test)

   ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ Failed Suites 1 ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯

    FAIL  src/playlist.test.ts [ src/playlist.test.ts ]
   Error: Cannot find module './playlist' imported from
   /home/you/creative-coding-2/coursework/playlist/src/playlist.test.ts
    ❯ src/playlist.test.ts:2:1
         1| import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
         2| import { Playlist } from './playlist';
          | ^

    Test Files  1 failed (1)
         Tests  no tests
   ```

   `Tests  no tests` at the bottom is the same failed suite you met in
   @sec-undo-experiment. The import had nowhere to go, so Vitest never reached
   your `it`.

3. Write the smallest class that answers that one test, in `src/playlist.ts`:

   ```ts
   export type Song = {
     title: string;
     artist: string;
   };

   export class Playlist {
     private songList: Song[] = [];

     toArray(): Song[] {
       return this.songList.slice();
     }
   }
   ```

   `npm test` turns green: `Tests  1 passed (1)`. `toArray` hands out a copy, so
   nobody can push a song into the playlist behind the class's back, exactly as
   the `items` getter of the undo stack did in @sec-undo-generic.

4. Another 14 sentences finish the playlist, and almost all of them need
   three songs on the list first. Put two small helpers and a `beforeEach` at the
   top of the `describe`, above your first `it`:

   ```ts
   describe('Playlist', () => {
     let playlist: Playlist;

     const addThreeSongs = (): void => {
       playlist.insertAtBeginning('Levitating', 'Dua Lipa');
       playlist.insertAtBeginning('Believer', 'Imagine Dragons');
       playlist.insertAtBeginning('Yellow', 'Coldplay');
     };

     const titles = (): string[] => playlist.toArray().map((song) => song.title);

     beforeEach(() => {
       playlist = new Playlist();
     });
   ```

   Add `beforeEach` to the import from `vitest`, and rewrite the first `it` to
   use the shared `playlist` instead of building its own. `map` runs your
   function on every item of an array and collects the results, so `titles()`
   turns three songs into three strings and a test can compare the order in one
   line. VS Code grays both helpers out until the tests below start calling
   them.

5. Write the five sentences about looking songs up and adding them at the front,
   one `it` at a time, and watch each one fail before you make it true:

   * an empty playlist finds nothing when you ask it for a title
   * three songs added at the beginning come out newest first
   * `find` hands back the whole song, title and artist together
   * `find` answers `null` for a title nobody added
   * a second song with a title that is already on the list is refused with
     `false`, and the playlist still holds its three songs

6. Then the four sentences about inserting behind a song you name:

   * a new song lands directly behind the title it names
   * naming the last song puts the new one at the end
   * a title nobody added is refused with `false`
   * a title that is already on the list is refused with `false`

7. And the five about removing:

   * the first song goes and the rest of the list closes up
   * a song in the middle goes
   * the last song goes
   * a title nobody added is refused with `false`
   * deleting the only song leaves an empty playlist

8. Here is the class once all 15 are green:

   ```ts
   export type Song = {
     title: string;
     artist: string;
   };

   export class Playlist {
     private songList: Song[] = [];

     find(title: string): Song | null {
       for (const song of this.songList) {
         if (song.title === title) {
           return song;
         }
       }
       return null;
     }

     insertAtBeginning(title: string, artist: string): boolean {
       if (this.find(title) !== null) {
         return false;
       }

       this.songList.unshift({ title, artist });
       return true;
     }

     insertAfter(afterTitle: string, title: string, artist: string): boolean {
       if (this.find(title) !== null) {
         return false;
       }

       const index = this.songList.findIndex((song) => song.title === afterTitle);
       if (index === -1) {
         return false;
       }

       this.songList.splice(index + 1, 0, { title, artist });
       return true;
     }

     delete(title: string): boolean {
       const index = this.songList.findIndex((song) => song.title === title);
       if (index === -1) {
         return false;
       }

       this.songList.splice(index, 1);
       return true;
     }

     toArray(): Song[] {
       return this.songList.slice();
     }
   }
   ```

   `findIndex` hands every item to your function and gives back the position of
   the first item your function said yes to, or `-1` when nothing matched.
   `splice(index, 0, item)` puts an item in at that position, and
   `splice(index, 1)` takes one out. Expected result:

   ```text
    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  15 passed (15)
   ```

The three methods that change the playlist answer with a `boolean` saying
whether anything happened, and `find` answers with a `Song | null`. That `null`
is the rule for the whole part: it means "you asked, and it is not there". The
caller has to look at the answer, which is why every test above checks the return
value and the list afterwards.

## The same playlist on nodes {#sec-linked-list-rewrite}

Now throw the array out. Nothing in `src/playlist.test.ts` changes, not one
character, because no test ever mentioned `songList`.

Put `Node<T>` at the top of `src/playlist.ts`, above `Song`, and replace the
private field:

```ts
export class Playlist {
  private head: Node<Song> | null = null;
```

Every method needs the same walk, so write it once as a private helper. It
starts at the head and follows `next` until either the title matches or the
chain runs out:

```ts
  private findNode(title: string): Node<Song> | null {
    let current = this.head;
    while (current !== null) {
      if (current.value.title === title) {
        return current;
      }

      current = current.next;
    }
    return null;
  }
```

`find` is that helper with the box unwrapped, because the outside world gets
songs and never nodes:

```ts
  find(title: string): Song | null {
    const node = this.findNode(title);
    if (node === null) {
      return null;
    }
    return node.value;
  }
```

`toArray` is the same walk again, collecting instead of comparing:

```ts
  toArray(): Song[] {
    const songs: Song[] = [];
    let current = this.head;
    while (current !== null) {
      songs.push(current.value);
      current = current.next;
    }
    return songs;
  }
```

### insertAtBeginning is two lines {#sec-linked-list-insert}

The `unshift` half of the timing experiment (@sec-linked-list-experiment) is the
cheapest thing this class does now. Build the node, point it at whatever the head
was, and make it the new head:

```ts
  insertAtBeginning(title: string, artist: string): boolean {
    if (this.find(title) !== null) {
      return false;
    }

    const newNode = new Node<Song>({ title, artist });
    newNode.next = this.head;
    this.head = newNode;
    return true;
  }
```

![Inserting at the beginning: the new node takes over the arrow the head used to
carry, and the head then points at the new node.](list-insert.svg){width=680}

The order of those two lines matters. Set `this.head` first and the arrow to the
old first node is gone, and the rest of the playlist goes with it. Watch out for
that in every method you write in this part, because once no arrow points at a
node any more there is no way back to it.

The rewiring is those same two lines on a playlist of 300 songs and on a playlist
of three. The duplicate check in front of it still walks the whole chain, so the
method as a whole is not free, but the part the experiment measured, making room
at the front, now costs nothing.

### insertAfter finds one node and puts a new one behind it {#sec-linked-list-insert-after}

`insertAfter` needs the node itself and not the song, which is exactly why
`findNode` is a separate helper:

```ts
  insertAfter(afterTitle: string, title: string, artist: string): boolean {
    if (this.find(title) !== null) {
      return false;
    }

    const afterNode = this.findNode(afterTitle);
    if (afterNode === null) {
      return false;
    }

    const newNode = new Node<Song>({ title, artist });
    newNode.next = afterNode.next;
    afterNode.next = newNode;
    return true;
  }
```

Two arrows change and the same trap applies, one step later. The new node has to
pick up the rest of the chain before `afterNode` lets go of it. The last song on
the list needs no special case: its `next` is `null`, the new node copies that
`null`, and the new node is the last one now.

### delete has a head to worry about {#sec-linked-list-delete}

Removing a node means making the node in front of it skip over it, and the first
node has nothing in front of it. That is the whole reason `delete` is longer than
the rest:

```ts
  delete(title: string): boolean {
    if (this.head === null) {
      return false;
    }

    if (this.head.value.title === title) {
      this.head = this.head.next;
      return true;
    }

    let previous = this.head;
    let current = this.head.next;
    while (current !== null) {
      if (current.value.title === title) {
        previous.next = current.next;
        return true;
      }

      previous = current;
      current = current.next;
    }

    return false;
  }
```

The head case moves the head one step forward. The general case walks with two
names instead of one, `previous` one node behind `current`, and hooks
`previous.next` onto whatever `current` was pointing at.

![Deleting from the middle: the node in front of the deleted song points at the
song behind it, and nothing points at the deleted node any
more.](list-delete.svg){width=740}

Look at the lower box in that picture. The deleted node still holds its song and
still points at the node behind it, and none of that matters, because no arrow
reaches it any more. A walk starting at the head can never arrive there, and
JavaScript throws the box away for you on its own schedule. Unhooking is all
deleting ever is.

Run `npm test`:

```text
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  15 passed (15)
```

Same 15, same file, and the storage underneath them is a different idea. That is
what a test suite is worth. The 15 sentences describe what a playlist does, they
never describe how it is stored, and that is why they could sit still through a
rewrite that touched every line of the class.

## Exercise: the playlist on the page {#sec-linked-list-exercise}

`Playlist` is tested and has never seen the DOM. Everything below happens in
`src/index.ts`, the only file in this project that touches the page.

1. Open the `index.html` you copied in and find the seven elements the next steps
   use: the paragraph with `id="chain"`, the form, the two text inputs for title
   and artist, the empty `<select id="afterTitle">`, the paragraph with
   `id="message"`, and the empty `<ul id="songs">`.

2. Replace `src/index.ts`. It starts with two imports, the seven lookups with
   `querySelector` and their element types, and one `if` with a
   `throw new Error(...)` that stops the app when any of them is missing.

   ```ts
   import './styles.css';
   import { Playlist } from './playlist';
   ```

3. The whole state of this app is one line:

   ```ts
   const playlist = new Playlist();
   ```

4. Write `renderChain()`. Empty the chain paragraph with `replaceChildren()`,
   then walk `playlist.toArray()` and append two elements per song: a
   `<span class="node">` with `${song.title} - ${song.artist}` in it and a
   `<span class="arrow">` holding `→`. After the loop, append one
   `<span class="node end">` reading `null`. An empty playlist therefore shows
   `null` and nothing else, which is exactly what the diagrams say it is.

5. Write `renderSongs()`. Empty the `<ul>`, then build one `<li>` per song with
   three children: a `<span class="song-title">` with the title, a plain `<span>`
   with the artist, and a **Delete** button. Give each button a `click` listener
   that calls `playlist.delete(song.title)`, clears the message paragraph, and
   calls `render()`.

6. Write `renderAfterOptions()`. Read `afterTitle.value` into a `const` first,
   empty the `<select>`, append one `<option>` with an empty value reading
   `the beginning`, then one `<option>` per song, and put the saved value back
   into `afterTitle.value` at the end. The research task has both properties an
   `<option>` needs. Saving the value first keeps the user's choice from jumping
   back to the top on every redraw.

7. Write `render()` with the three calls in it, and call it once at the end of
   the file so the fresh page already shows an empty chain.

8. Give the form a `submit` listener. Call `preventDefault()`, read both inputs
   with `.trim()`, and write `'Please enter a title and an artist.'` into the
   message paragraph when either is empty. Otherwise insert: an empty
   `afterTitle.value` means `insertAtBeginning`, any other value means
   `insertAfter` with that value as the first argument. When the insert answers
   `false`, write
   `` `The playlist already has a song called "${title}".` `` into the message
   and leave the handler. When it answers `true`, clear the message, clear both
   inputs, and call `render()`.

9. Run `npm start` and check all of it. Expected results:

   * a fresh page shows a chain of one gray `null` box and nothing else
   * adding *Levitating* by *Dua Lipa*, then *Believer* by *Imagine Dragons*,
     then *Yellow* by *Coldplay*, each of them with **Insert after** on
     *the beginning*, gives the chain
     `Yellow - Coldplay → Believer - Imagine Dragons → Levitating - Dua Lipa → null`
   * adding *Bad Guy* by *Billie Eilish* with **Insert after** on *Believer*
     drops it between *Believer* and *Levitating*, and the dropdown grows a
     *Bad Guy* entry in the same place
   * adding *Yellow* a second time changes nothing on the page and writes
     `The playlist already has a song called "Yellow".` into the message
   * submitting with an empty artist field writes
     `Please enter a title and an artist.` and adds nothing
   * **Delete** on the *Believer* row removes it and closes the chain up
     around it

10. Run `npm test` and expect `Tests  15 passed (15)`. Add the `verify` script
    with its three checks to `package.json` as in every new app, run
    `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

**Move a song to the top.** Add `moveToFront(title: string): boolean` to
`Playlist`. Write the tests first: moving the middle song puts it in front and
keeps the other two in their old order, moving the first song changes nothing,
and a title nobody added answers `false`. You already own both halves of the
job, `delete` and `insertAtBeginning`, so the method can be four lines. Then put
a **To top** button next to every **Delete** button.

**Point backwards too.** Give each node a second pointer, `previous`, so the
chain can be walked from either end. Every method that rewires `next` now
rewires `previous` as well, and the head case of `delete` needs one more line.
That structure is called a doubly linked list, and it is worth building once so
you feel what the second pointer costs in every single method.
:::
